standard_prerequisites.name: Pointed predicate and pointed map
standard_prerequisites.statement: A pointed predicate over (A,a_0) is a family R : A \to \type together with r_0 : R(a_0), and a pointed map is a family of maps respecting the base points.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the objects among which the four conditions are stated (source lines 1152-1155).

standard_prerequisites.name: Identity system at a point
standard_prerequisites.statement: R with r_0 is an identity system at a_0 when for every D : \prd{b:A} R(b) \to \type and d : D(a_0,r_0) there is f : \prd{b:A}{r:R(b)} D(b,r) with f(a_0,r_0) = d.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is condition 1 of the counted theorem and the hypothesis of the first implication.

standard_prerequisites.name: Contractibility of a type of pointed maps
standard_prerequisites.statement: Contractibility is the combination of inhabitation and the equality of any two of its elements, obtained here through function extensionality and the path types of \Sigma-types.
standard_prerequisites.use: Condition 2 and the derivation of condition 3 from it (source lines 1175-1185).

standard_prerequisites.name: Transport and \Sigma-types preserving equivalences
standard_prerequisites.statement: Transport in a family of types is an equivalence, and a \Sigma-type formed over an equivalence is again an equivalence.
standard_prerequisites.use: Condition 3 is turned into condition 4 with these two facts (source line 1188).

core_obligations: From condition 1 build a pointed map R \to S for any pointed predicate S, and show any two such pointed maps are equal, so that ppmap(R,S) is contractible (source lines 1168-1174).

From condition 2 take S(b) \defeq (a_0 = b) and derive a pointed map in both directions between R and S, whose composites are identities because the pointed-map types ppmap(R,R) and ppmap(S,S) are contractible (source lines 1176-1185).
From condition 3 deduce that \sm{b:A} R(b) is contractible, transporting the contractibility of the path type through the equivalence of \Sigma-types (source line 1188).

From condition 4, given D and d, express D on the contractible total type, transport d along a uniform path family, and check the base-point computation to obtain f with f(a_0,r_0) = d (source lines 1190-1192).

proof_roadmap.step: Condition 1 implies condition 2: build the pointed map and prove the pointed-map type a mere proposition.
Condition 2 implies condition 3: use the path type as a pointed predicate and contractibility of the pointed-map types.
Condition 3 implies condition 4: transport contractibility of the path type through the equivalence of \Sigma-types.
Condition 4 implies condition 1: transport d along the uniform path family of the contractible total type.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled theorem at source lines 1152-1160 (book Theorem 5.8.2): four conditions on a pointed predicate over a pointed type, namely being an identity system, having a contractible type of pointed maps into every pointed predicate, having all the transport maps out of the loop space be equivalences, and having a contractible total type, are logically equivalent. The statement lists the four conditions and nothing else, while the proof (source lines 1167-1193) runs the cycle in one direction only and must construct, for each implication, the auxiliary pointed predicate and the two pointed maps that make the argument go through: for the first implication it turns the identity-system elimination into inhabitation and then into a mere proposition by applying elimination to the equality of any two pointed maps; for the second it uses (a_0 = b) as the auxiliary family and gets the composites to be identities from the contractibility of the pointed-map types ppmap(R,R) and ppmap(S,S); the third goes through the equivalence of \Sigma-types; the fourth has to transport the given element along a uniform path family of the contractible total type and check the base-point computation. Only the derived direction of each implication is proved, so the chapter's observation that the four conditions are also logically equivalent as propositions is used, not proved.
